Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

(CNN) -- A U.N. special investigator called for the resignation of top Kenyan officials and sweeping changes in the country's security forces to end reported widespread killings by police across the African nation. The report urged President Mwai Kibaki to publicly acknowledge his commitment to ending the killings. "The special rapporteur concluded that police in Kenya frequently execute individuals and that a climate of impunity prevails," Philip Alston said in a report a recently submitted to the U.N. Human Rights Council in Geneva. "Most troubling is the existence of police death squads operating on the orders of senior police officials and charged with eliminating suspected leaders and members of criminal organizations." The report calls for the resignation of Kenya's attorney general and the immediate replacement of the police commissioner. It also says Kenyan President Mwai Kibaki should publicly acknowledge his commitment to ending unlawful killings by the police. The Kenyan government expressed its "deep displeasure" with the report, questioning the special investigator's "approach, conduct and method of work." "The government expresses grave concern regarding the allegations contained in the report by the special rapporteur," said Alfred Mutua, a spokesman for the Kenyan government. "His questioning of the very basis of the Kenyan state and, in particular, its institutions is totally unacceptable and impinges on Kenya's sovereignty." Alston also accused government security forces of torturing and killing hundreds of men in a March 2008 crackdown on a militia in the Mt. Elgon district, in western Kenya. And he said there was compelling evidence that what he called police death squads were operating in Nairobi and Central Province with a mandate to "exterminate" suspected Mungiki gang members. "These are not "rogue" squads, but police who are acting on the explicit orders of their superiors," he said. The Mungiki militia, which is loyal to Kibaki's Kikuyu tribe, began as a religious sect, but over the years has morphed into a gang that runs protection rackets -- particularly in the slums. The U.N. investigator suggested Kibaki acknowledge the alleged police killings and commit to stop them. He also advocated creating an independent civilian police oversight body, and said the prosecutor of the International Criminal Court should investigate violence after the 2007 election. He urged the government to create a witness protection program as well. Alston, who investigates human-rights problems around the world for the United Nations, traveled to Kenya at the government's invitation. He stayed for 10 days in mid-February while 100 interviews were conducted in the U.N. member nation. There is hope for Kenya despite his criticism, Alston said. "While the existing situation is bad, it is far from intractable," the report says. "If it so chooses, Kenya can significantly reduce the prevalence of unlawful killings."

The report urged President Mwai Kibaki to publicly affirm his commitment to ending the killings.

Human Rights Council in Geneva. “Most troubling is the existence of police death squads operating on the orders of senior police officials and charged with eliminating suspected leaders and members of criminal organizations.”

The report calls for the resignation of Kenya’s attorney general and the immediate replacement of the police commissioner. It also says Kibaki should publicly acknowledge his commitment to ending unlawful killings by the police.

The Kenyan government expressed its “deep displeasure” with the report, questioning the special investigator’s “approach, conduct and method of work.”

“The government expresses grave concern regarding the allegations contained in the report by the special rapporteur,” said Alfred Mutua, a spokesman for the Kenyan government. “His questioning of the very basis of the Kenyan state and, in particular, its institutions is totally unacceptable and impinges on Kenya’s sovereignty.”

Alston also accused government security forces of torturing and killing hundreds of men during a March 2008 crackdown on a militia in the Mt. Elgon district of western Kenya. He said there was compelling evidence that what he described as police death squads were operating in Nairobi and Central Province with a mandate to “exterminate” suspected members of the Mungiki gang.

“These are not ‘rogue’ squads, but police who are acting on the explicit orders of their superiors,” he said.

The Mungiki militia, which is loyal to Kibaki’s Kikuyu tribe, began as a religious sect but has, over the years, evolved into a gang that runs protection rackets, particularly in the slums.

The U.N. investigator suggested that Kibaki acknowledge the alleged police killings and commit to stopping them. He also advocated the creation of an independent civilian police oversight body and said the prosecutor of the International Criminal Court should investigate the violence that followed the 2007 election. He further urged the government to establish a witness protection program.

Alston, who investigates human rights problems around the world for the United Nations, traveled to Kenya at the government’s invitation. He spent 10 days there in mid-February, during which 100 interviews were conducted in the U.N. member nation.

Despite his criticism, Alston said there is hope for Kenya.

“While the existing situation is bad, it is far from intractable,” the report says. “If it so chooses, Kenya can significantly reduce the prevalence of unlawful killings.”

(CNN) — A United Nations special investigator has urged senior Kenyan officials to step down and called for major reforms of the country’s security services in response to reports of extensive police killings throughout Kenya.

The report said President Mwai Kibaki should make a public declaration that he is committed to stopping the killings. Philip Alston, in a report recently presented to the U.N. Human Rights Council in Geneva, said the special rapporteur found that Kenyan police often carry out executions and that a culture of impunity exists.

Alston wrote that the most disturbing finding was the presence of police death squads allegedly acting under instructions from high-ranking police officials and tasked with killing suspected leaders and members of criminal groups.

The report demanded the resignation of Kenya’s attorney general and the immediate removal and replacement of the police commissioner. It also stated that Kibaki should publicly affirm his determination to end unlawful killings by police.

Kenya’s government reacted angrily, saying it was “deeply displeased” with the report and challenging the special investigator’s “approach, conduct and method of work.”

Alfred Mutua, a Kenyan government spokesman, said the government was seriously concerned about the accusations in the special rapporteur’s report. He added that Alston’s questioning of the foundations of the Kenyan state, especially its institutions, was “totally unacceptable” and interfered with Kenya’s sovereignty.

Alston also alleged that government security forces tortured and killed hundreds of men during a March 2008 operation against a militia in the Mt. Elgon district of western Kenya. He further said there was strong evidence that what he described as police death squads were active in Nairobi and Central Province, with orders to “exterminate” suspected members of the Mungiki gang.

“These are not ‘rogue’ squads, but police who are acting on the explicit orders of their superiors,” Alston said.

The Mungiki militia, aligned with Kibaki’s Kikuyu ethnic group, originally emerged as a religious movement. Over time, however, it developed into a gang involved in protection rackets, especially in slum areas.

The U.N. investigator recommended that Kibaki recognize the alleged police killings and pledge to end them. He also called for the establishment of an independent civilian body to monitor the police. In addition, Alston said the prosecutor of the International Criminal Court should examine the violence that followed Kenya’s 2007 election, and he urged the government to set up a witness protection program.

Alston, whose U.N. role involves investigating human rights concerns worldwide, visited Kenya at the invitation of the government. He spent 10 days there in mid-February, during which 100 interviews were carried out in the U.N. member country.

Despite his criticism, Alston said Kenya’s situation was not hopeless. The report stated that although current conditions are serious, they are not impossible to fix, and that Kenya could sharply reduce unlawful killings if it decides to do so.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a CNN-style news article about a U.N. special rapporteur accusing Kenyan police of widespread extrajudicial killings and calling for reforms.
counterfactuals.output:
**U.N. expert accuses Kenyan police of widespread extrajudicial killings, urges sweeping reforms**

**NAIROBI, Kenya** — A United Nations special rapporteur has accused Kenyan police of carrying out widespread extrajudicial killings and operating with near-total impunity, calling for urgent reforms to the country’s security services and justice system.

The rapporteur said evidence gathered from witnesses, human rights groups and official sources pointed to a pattern of unlawful killings by police, including suspected executions of criminal suspects and alleged members of outlawed groups. The findings raise serious concerns about accountability within Kenya’s law enforcement agencies and the government’s willingness to address abuses, the U.N. expert said.

“These are not isolated incidents,” the rapporteur said, describing the killings as part of a broader system in which officers accused of serious abuses are rarely investigated or prosecuted.

The report calls on Kenyan authorities to establish independent mechanisms to investigate police killings, strengthen civilian oversight, protect witnesses and ensure that officers implicated in unlawful deaths face prosecution. It also urges reforms to the chain of command and improved record-keeping around arrests, detentions and police operations.

Kenyan officials have previously defended police actions as necessary to combat violent crime and organized gangs, while saying abuses are investigated when credible evidence is presented. But rights groups have long accused security forces of using anti-crime operations as cover for illegal executions, particularly in poor urban neighborhoods.

Human rights organizations welcomed the rapporteur’s findings, saying they echo years of documentation by local activists and families of victims. They said the U.N. intervention should increase pressure on the government to end impunity and provide justice for those killed.

The allegations come amid broader concerns over police conduct in Kenya, where security forces have repeatedly faced criticism over excessive force, arbitrary arrests and deaths in custody. Activists say fear of retaliation often prevents witnesses and victims’ families from reporting abuses.

The rapporteur said meaningful reform would require political will at the highest levels of government, warning that failure to act would further erode public trust in the police and the courts.

“Kenya cannot build the rule of law while tolerating unlawful killings by those sworn to uphold it,” the U.N. expert said.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

**U.N. Expert Accuses Kenyan Police of Operating Death Squads; Government Rejects Findings**

*Nairobi* — A United Nations human rights investigator has accused Kenyan police of carrying out widespread extrajudicial killings and operating “death squads,” prompting a sharp rejection from the Kenyan government.

Philip Alston, the U.N. Special Rapporteur on extrajudicial, summary or arbitrary executions, said after a fact-finding mission to Kenya that police units had been responsible for systematic killings, particularly in operations targeting suspected members of the outlawed Mungiki sect and other criminal suspects. He said the killings were often followed by official denials, poor investigations, or no accountability at all.

Alston’s findings, presented to the U.N. Human Rights Council, described a pattern in which suspects were arrested or abducted, later found dead, or simply disappeared. He alleged that officers acted with near-total impunity and that state institutions had failed to investigate or prosecute those responsible.

“The evidence points to the existence of police death squads,” Alston said in substance, arguing that the killings were not isolated incidents but part of a broader policing culture that tolerated unlawful executions.

The U.N. expert was especially critical of Kenya’s senior law-enforcement leadership. He called for major reforms, including stronger civilian oversight of the police, independent investigations into killings, witness protection, and accountability for senior officials who failed to prevent or punish abuses. Alston also urged the resignation or removal of top officials, including the police commissioner and the attorney general, saying they had failed to address the problem.

Kenyan officials rejected the report’s conclusions, accusing Alston of relying on unverified claims and of ignoring the security challenges posed by violent criminal gangs. The government denied that police operated death squads and said any abuses by individual officers should not be presented as official policy.

Authorities argued that police had been confronting dangerous criminal organizations and insisted that Kenya had mechanisms to investigate misconduct. Government representatives also criticized the tone of the U.N. findings, saying they damaged the country’s image and undermined police efforts to maintain order.

Human rights groups in Kenya, however, said Alston’s findings matched years of documentation by local organizations, which had recorded numerous cases of suspected extrajudicial executions and disappearances. Activists called on the government to implement the recommendations and ensure that witnesses and investigators were protected.

The controversy placed renewed pressure on Kenya to reform its police service, long accused by rights groups of corruption, brutality, and impunity. Alston’s report became one of the most prominent international condemnations of Kenya’s security forces and added momentum to calls for independent police oversight and justice for victims’ families.

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose an article summarizing a U.N. investigator’s report urging President Mwai Kibaki to address unlawful police killings, replace top security officials, and create oversight mechanisms.
counterfactuals.output:
**U.N. Investigator Urges Kibaki to Act on Police Killings in Kenya**

A United Nations investigator has called on Kenyan President Mwai Kibaki to confront what he described as widespread unlawful killings by police, warning that impunity within the country’s security services has seriously undermined the rule of law.

In a sharply critical report, the U.N. special rapporteur on extrajudicial, summary or arbitrary executions urged Kibaki’s government to take decisive action, including replacing senior security officials, establishing independent oversight bodies, and ensuring that police accused of killings are investigated and prosecuted.

The report said Kenyan police had been implicated in numerous unlawful killings, including suspected executions carried out during operations against criminal gangs and in the aftermath of political violence. It argued that the problem was not limited to isolated misconduct by individual officers, but reflected deeper institutional failures and a culture in which police could act with little fear of accountability.

The investigator called for the dismissal or resignation of top officials responsible for internal security and policing, saying meaningful reform would be impossible while those overseeing the system remained in place. He also recommended the creation of credible civilian oversight mechanisms to investigate complaints against police, monitor abuses, and restore public confidence.

According to the report, existing systems for investigating police misconduct were inadequate because they relied too heavily on the police to police themselves. Victims’ families and human rights groups, it said, often faced intimidation, delays, or outright refusal when seeking justice.

The U.N. investigator also urged the government to strengthen witness protection, improve record-keeping on deaths in police custody or during police operations, and make public the results of investigations into alleged extrajudicial killings.

The findings placed new pressure on Kibaki’s administration, which had already faced domestic and international criticism over security-force abuses and the handling of post-election violence. Human rights organizations have long accused Kenyan police of carrying out summary executions, particularly during crackdowns on groups such as the Mungiki sect.

The report emphasized that tackling violent crime and maintaining public order cannot justify unlawful killings. It said Kenya must ensure that all security operations comply with national and international law, and that officers responsible for abuses are held accountable through transparent legal processes.

While the Kenyan government has previously denied that extrajudicial killings are official policy, the U.N. report argued that the scale of the allegations and the lack of prosecutions point to systemic impunity. It warned that failure to act would deepen public mistrust and weaken efforts to reform the police.

The investigator’s recommendations amount to a direct challenge to Kibaki’s government: remove officials who have failed to prevent abuses, create independent oversight, and end the perception that police killings can occur without consequences.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.output:
NAIROBI — Kenyan security forces have been accused by human rights groups and witnesses of torturing and killing civilians during past crackdowns on armed groups, including the Mungiki sect and militias operating in the Mt. Elgon region.

The allegations relate to security operations carried out in the 2000s, when police and military units were deployed to counter violent gangs and insurgent groups blamed for killings, extortion and intimidation. Rights organisations said the operations often swept up civilians, with detainees allegedly beaten, tortured, forcibly disappeared or killed outside the judicial process.

In Mt. Elgon, near Kenya’s border with Uganda, security forces launched operations against the Sabaot Land Defence Force, a militia accused of atrocities linked to land disputes. Human rights monitors alleged that soldiers and police tortured suspects and residents during interrogations, including beatings and other abuses. Some detainees were later reported dead or missing.

Separate allegations were made during crackdowns on Mungiki, a banned sect and criminal network accused of murders, extortion and political violence. Rights groups said police carried out extrajudicial killings and enforced disappearances of suspected members and young men from affected communities.

Kenyan authorities have in the past said security operations were necessary to restore order and protect civilians from militia violence. Officials have also denied or disputed some allegations of systematic abuse, while promising investigations in certain cases.

Human rights campaigners say accountability has been limited, with few prosecutions of security personnel despite repeated calls for independent investigations. They argue that failure to address past abuses has deepened mistrust between communities and the state, and has undermined the rule of law.

The allegations remain a prominent part of Kenya’s human rights record, cited by local and international organisations as examples of excessive force and impunity during internal security operations.

## Kenya rejects U.N. report accusing police of executions and operating death squads

**Nairobi, Kenya** — Kenya has rejected a United Nations human rights report accusing its police force of carrying out extrajudicial executions, benefiting from widespread impunity and operating death squads allegedly protected by senior officials.

The report, prepared by the U.N. special rapporteur on extrajudicial, summary or arbitrary executions, alleges that Kenyan police have killed suspects without trial, targeted criminal gangs and political opponents, and avoided accountability through intimidation, cover-ups and official inaction.

Kenyan officials dismissed the findings, saying the report was biased, inaccurate and based on unverified claims. The government said it remained committed to the rule of law and accused the U.N. investigator of overstepping his mandate and failing to take into account Kenya’s security challenges.

The U.N. report paints a starkly different picture, alleging that unlawful killings by police were not isolated incidents but part of a broader pattern. It says security units operated with the knowledge, or at least the tolerance, of senior figures in government and law enforcement.

According to the report, police units allegedly executed suspected members of criminal gangs, including the Mungiki sect, a banned group long accused of extortion, murder and organized violence. The report also cites killings linked to Kenya’s post-election violence, when more than 1,000 people were killed and hundreds of thousands displaced after the disputed 2007 presidential election.

The U.N. investigator said Kenya’s justice system had failed to hold police accountable, creating a culture in which officers accused of unlawful killings were rarely prosecuted. Witnesses and human rights defenders who documented abuses also faced threats, the report said.

“Impunity is the central problem,” the report said, arguing that police accountability mechanisms were weak, compromised or unwilling to act against senior officers.

The report called for sweeping reforms, including independent investigations into alleged police killings, stronger witness protection, and accountability for senior officials accused of enabling or ignoring abuses.

Kenya’s government rejected the recommendations, saying the country had internal mechanisms to investigate misconduct. Officials argued that police operate in a difficult environment, confronting heavily armed gangs, organized crime networks and violent militias.

Human rights groups in Kenya and abroad welcomed the U.N. report, saying it confirmed years of documented allegations against security forces. They urged the government to allow independent investigations and prosecute officers implicated in unlawful killings.

“The government cannot simply dismiss these findings,” one rights advocate said. “There must be accountability for victims and protection for witnesses.”

The allegations are likely to deepen tensions between Nairobi and international human rights bodies, which have repeatedly criticized Kenya’s handling of police abuses and political violence.

Kenya has long been considered a key regional ally for Western governments, particularly on counterterrorism and security operations in East Africa. But rights groups say that cooperation has too often overshadowed concerns about abuses by security forces.

The U.N. report warns that without reforms, extrajudicial killings and police impunity will continue to undermine public trust in Kenya’s institutions.

For families of alleged victims, the report has renewed calls for justice.

Many say their relatives were arrested by police and later found dead, while others disappeared without explanation. In numerous cases, rights groups say, official investigations were never opened or quietly stalled.

Kenyan authorities maintain that they do not sanction unlawful killings and say any officer found guilty of misconduct will face the law.

But the U.N. report concludes that accountability must reach beyond individual officers, arguing that senior officials who tolerated or failed to prevent alleged death squad operations should also be investigated.

The dispute now places renewed pressure on Kenya to demonstrate whether it is willing to confront claims of state-sponsored violence — or continue rejecting outside scrutiny as interference.
